newsitem.title: INDIA: Train attack victims lie in India paddy field.
newsitem.headline: Train attack victims lie in India paddy field.

text.p: Dozens of mutilated bodies lay on a soft rice paddy field on Tuesday, victims of a vicious attack on a passenger train in northeastern India.

A Reuter correspondent saw severed arms and legs scattered about some three dozen bodies, including small children, stretched out on the damp ground. Some were still bleeding. They appeared torn and crushed, not charred.
Authorities said 59 bodies had so far been recovered from the train wreckage in Sensapani town, some 200 km (125 miles) west of the biggest city in Assam state, Guwahati.
Officials blamed Bodo tribal separatists for the attack.
Three carriages were completely destroyed by twin bombs which exploded on the train track on Monday evening. Little beyond a jumble of twisted steel remained of the coaches.
Authorities said as many as 300 people, most of them heading to the Indian capital New Delhi for the New Year holiday, may have been travelling in the coaches.
Two other carriages were hurled off the track by the blasts, which officials said were set off by remote control.
Eighteen hours after the accident, emergency workers appeared to be concentrating on repairing the ruptured rail line which links India's distant northeast from the rest of the country.
Workers were using two cranes to try to restore the mangled rails. Dozens of police holding rifles guarded the bodies in the field. But no medical workers could be seen near the wreckage.
The site of the attack is two km (1.3 miles) from Fakiragram and accessible from that village only by foot.
The nearest road leads over a bamboo bridge and through a sandy river bed to reach Kokrajhar, some 18 km (12 miles) to the east.
Residents said the area was dominated by Bengali-speaking Hindus, who indigenous Bodos say have stood in the way of their decade-old drive for a homeland.
